\section[gacchāmi]{\sk{गच्छामि} (gacchāmi) — \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} (taking leave)}

\label{lesson:SA-C04-gacchami}



\begin{quote}
Sanskrit has no casual \textquotedblleft{}bye.\textquotedblright{} Like its daughters, it takes leave by saying \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} — and the verb is a cousin of English \emph{come} and \emph{go}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{gac · chā · mi}. Both \emph{c} sounds are the \emph{ch} of \emph{church}, and the doubling is real — hold it a moment longer than one \emph{ch}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{gacchāmi} (\textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{}) is from the root \emph{gam} (\textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}) — the very root you met in Chapter 1's \emph{svāgatam} (= \emph{su} + \emph{āgata}, \textquotedblleft{}well come,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{ā} + \emph{gam}). That root is Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*g\textsuperscript{w}em-}, the ancestor of English \textbf{come} (and, via Latin \emph{venīre}, of \emph{venue}, \emph{convene}). To leave politely one says \emph{gacchāmi} (\textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{}) or, more gracefully, \emph{āgacchāmi} (\textquotedblleft{}I {[}shall{]} come {[}back{]}\textquotedblright{}) — the same \textquotedblleft{}promise of return\textquotedblright{} the modern languages kept.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gacchāmi\textquotedblright{} — I go
  \item the root and its Chapter-1 cousin (\emph{gam}; \emph{svāgatam}, \textquotedblleft{}well come\textquotedblright{})
  \item the English cousin of \emph{gam} (\textbf{come})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Sanskrit take leave, and what root is \emph{gacchāmi} from? (By saying \textquotedblleft{}I go,\textquotedblright{} \emph{gacchāmi}; the root \emph{gam}, PIE \emph{*g\textsuperscript{w}em-}, cousin of English \textbf{come}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[punaḥ]{\sk{पुनः} (punaḥ) — \textquotedblleft{}again,\textquotedblright{} the seed of \textquotedblleft{}till we meet again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:SA-C04-punah}



\begin{quote}
One small word turns a leave-taking into a promise of return.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{pu · naḥ}, closing on the soft breathed \emph{-ḥ}. Before certain following sounds that breath turns into an \emph{r}: \emph{punar-}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{punaḥ} (\textquotedblleft{}again, back, once more\textquotedblright{}) is a native Sanskrit adverb (its combining form is \emph{punar-}, as in \emph{punar-janma}, \textquotedblleft{}rebirth\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}birth again\textquotedblright{}). It has no tidy single English cognate, but its work is one English shares: it turns a parting into \textquotedblleft{}see you \textbf{again}.\textquotedblright{} Add it to \emph{darśana} (\textquotedblleft{}seeing\textquotedblright{}) and you get the graceful Sanskrit farewell of the next lesson.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}punaḥ\textquotedblright{}
  \item its combining form and a word from it (\emph{punar-}; \emph{punarjanma}, \textquotedblleft{}rebirth\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{punaḥ} mean, and what is its combining form? (\textquotedblleft{}Again\textquotedblright{}; \emph{punar-}, as in \emph{punarjanma}, \textquotedblleft{}rebirth.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ra]{\sk{र} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S110-letter-ra}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{◌ा} · \sk{म} · \sk{◌ु}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{र}}
\textbf{\sk{र}} — \emph{ra}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{r}, it is \textbf{ra}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a top-to-bottom stem curling clockwise around the lower loop
  \item a diagonal tail
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say this word, and \sk{र} is one of the shapes inside it — the rest of its shapes are still ahead of you, so here the character stands on its own:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{namaskāraḥ} — hello (lit. \textquotedblleft{}the making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{र}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the headline junction, descend the stem, and curl left and clockwise around the lower loop to the tail junction
  \item \textbf{2.} lift at that junction and draw the diagonal tail down-right
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified three-stroke teaching form; another animated learner source joins the loop and diagonal tail
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\sk{र}-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{र} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{र}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{र} three times, saying \emph{ra} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{र} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{र}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ra}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[punardarśanāya]{\sk{पुनर्दर्शनाय} (punar-darśanāya) — \textquotedblleft{}until we meet again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:SA-C04-punar-darshanaya}



\begin{quote}
The graceful Sanskrit goodbye — \textquotedblleft{}for the sake of seeing {[}you{]} again.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{pu · nar · dar · śa · nā · ya}. Six even beats; \emph{ś} is the \emph{sh} of \emph{ship}; the long \emph{ā} falls in the fifth.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{punardarśanāya} = \emph{punar} (\textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{darśana} (\textquotedblleft{}seeing, sight, vision\textquotedblright{}) in the \textbf{dative} case (\emph{-āya}, \textquotedblleft{}for the sake of\textquotedblright{}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{for seeing {[}you{]} again},\textquotedblright{} i.e. \textquotedblleft{}until we meet again.\textquotedblright{} The word \emph{darśana} is deep: it is \textquotedblleft{}seeing\textquotedblright{} in the sense of \emph{beholding} — the \emph{darśan} one takes of a deity or a revered person, and the name of the six \emph{darśanas}, the schools of Indian philosophy (\textquotedblleft{}ways of seeing\textquotedblright{}). So this farewell promises not just a meeting but a \emph{beholding} to come.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the dative \textquotedblleft{}for the sake of\textquotedblright{}}]
The ending \emph{-āya} is the dative singular — \textquotedblleft{}to / for.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Darśana} (a seeing) $\to$ \emph{darśanāya} (for a seeing). You will meet the cases one at a time; this is your first, the \textquotedblleft{}for-the-purpose-of\textquotedblright{} case.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}punar-darśanāya\textquotedblright{}
  \item its literal meaning (\textquotedblleft{}for seeing {[}you{]} again\textquotedblright{})
  \item what \emph{darśana} means beyond \textquotedblleft{}seeing\textquotedblright{} (a beholding; the \emph{darśan} of a deity)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{punar-darśanāya} literally mean, and what case gives the \textquotedblleft{}for\textquotedblright{}? (\textquotedblleft{}For seeing again\textquotedblright{}; the dative \emph{-āya}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śvaḥ]{\sk{श्वः} (śvaḥ) — \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:SA-C04-shvah}



\begin{quote}
A goodbye with a date on it — and a word that, unlike Hindi's \emph{kal}, means only one day.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{śvaḥ} — one beat: the \emph{sh} of \emph{ship} pushed straight into \emph{v}, then the soft breathed \emph{-ḥ}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{śvaḥ} (\textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}) is from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*\'{k}es-} (\textquotedblleft{}tomorrow / morning\textquotedblright{}). Where the modern Indian languages muddle \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}yesterday\textquotedblright{} into one word (Hindi \emph{kal}, Bengali \emph{kāl}, from \emph{kāla} \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{}), classical Sanskrit kept them \textbf{separate and precise}: \emph{śvaḥ} is \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} and \emph{hyaḥ} is \textquotedblleft{}yesterday\textquotedblright{} — two distinct words. \textquotedblleft{}See you tomorrow\textquotedblright{} is \emph{śvaḥ punar-darśanam} (\textquotedblleft{}tomorrow, a seeing-again\textquotedblright{}) or \emph{śvaḥ drakṣyāmi} (\textquotedblleft{}tomorrow I shall see {[}you{]}\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Sanskrit's precision}]
That the daughters blurred \emph{śvaḥ} / \emph{hyaḥ} into a single \emph{kal} is a small window into language change: the modern tongues traded precision for economy, letting tense carry the load. Sanskrit, the older layer, still keeps the two days apart.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}śvaḥ\textquotedblright{} (tomorrow) and \textquotedblleft{}hyaḥ\textquotedblright{} (yesterday)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{} — \emph{śvaḥ punar-darśanam}
  \item how this differs from Hindi/Bengali \emph{kal} (Sanskrit keeps the two days distinct)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{śvaḥ} mean, and how does Sanskrit differ from Hindi here? (\textquotedblleft{}Tomorrow\textquotedblright{}; Sanskrit keeps \emph{śvaḥ} \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} and \emph{hyaḥ} \textquotedblleft{}yesterday\textquotedblright{} separate, where Hindi merges them into \emph{kal}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pa]{\sk{प} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S113-letter-pa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{म} · \sk{◌ु} · \sk{र}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{प}}
\textbf{\sk{प}} — \emph{pa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{p}, it is \textbf{pa}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a left stem curving around the lower bowl to its upper-right junction
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{प} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{पुनः}} \emph{punaḥ} — again
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{प}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} descend the left stem, then curve right around the lower bowl and rise to its upper-right junction without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified three-stroke teaching form; everyday handwriting may join or simplify the bowl differently
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\sk{प}-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{प} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{पुनः}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{प} three times, saying \emph{pa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{प} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[Practice]{Chapter 4 — The farewells}

\label{lesson:SA-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Three ways to part — the ancestors of the modern Indian goodbyes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item taking leave — \emph{gacchāmi} (\textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}until we meet again\textquotedblright{} — \emph{punar-darśanāya}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{} — \emph{śvaḥ punar-darśanam}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{How to answer: the atoms}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the verb \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{} and its Ch-1 cousin (\emph{gam}; \emph{svāgatam})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} and its combining form (\emph{punaḥ} / \emph{punar-})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} vs. \textquotedblleft{}yesterday\textquotedblright{} (Sanskrit keeps \emph{śvaḥ} / \emph{hyaḥ} distinct)
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: the roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gam} \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*g\textsuperscript{w}em-} $\to$ English \textbf{come}
  \item \emph{punaḥ / punar-} \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} ($\to$ \emph{punarjanma}, \textquotedblleft{}rebirth\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{darśana} \textquotedblleft{}a seeing / beholding\textquotedblright{} (the six \emph{darśanas} of philosophy)
  \item \emph{śvaḥ} \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} \emph{hyaḥ} \textquotedblleft{}yesterday\textquotedblright{} — kept separate, unlike Hindi \emph{kal}
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
You're taking leave and expect to see someone tomorrow. Give the graceful goodbye, and specify tomorrow. (\emph{Punar-darśanāya} — or \emph{śvaḥ punar-darśanam}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
